source.title: When In-Distribution Gains Fail: Evaluating Weak-to-Strong Reward Models under Preference Shift
source.authors: Khoi M. Le; C. Trinh; Phong Nguyen; Cong-Duy T. Nguyen; A. Lưu; Chun-Yan Miao; See-Kiong Ng; T. Nguyen

page_placements.theme: Weak-label fine-tuning leaves the strong student below its own pre-fine-tuning performance or erodes its representations

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text, but their labeled columns and the paper’s accompanying prose allow the results below to be assigned.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies weak-to-strong reward-model training and reports PGR and transfer results, while showing that in-distribution gains do not ensure transfer across preference datasets. This refines the scope of the weak-to-strong effect; the measured distribution-shift results also bear directly on V4.
record.gate_note: Recorded explicitly described W2S, PGR, transfer, method-comparison, ablation, and representation-probe results. The paper reports many additional per-dataset and per-model results in Tables 1, 7, and 9–14; not every table cell is separately transcribed here. Results about A NCHOR’s training overhead and the CKA/CCA plots are not included as claim rows because they do not themselves measure weak-to-strong improvement or preference behavior.
record.test_reason: Trains 8B reward-model students on 1B/1.7B weak-teacher preference labels across 12 source datasets in two families. It reports in-distribution PGR/WRG against weak and strong-ceiling baselines (V1, V3), compares confidence loss, SEAM, ANCHOR and preservation controls with naive W2S (V2), and evaluates zero-shot cross-dataset transfer (V4). It argues in-distribution W2S gains overstate reliability under preference shift. Not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that ANCHOR is best or tied in 41 of 60 comparisons, not uniformly dominant. Also add that the authors attribute much of the residual OOD deficit to source–target transfer difficulty that persists even under gold supervision.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-teacher preference labels to train a stronger reward model and reports PGR, as in the original W2S work, but focuses on cross-dataset preference-domain shift. It adds transfer-aware metrics and proposes representation anchoring; it does not replicate the original study’s full task suite.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model family, source and target dataset, training method, anchoring coefficient, and anchored layer. The paper reports that stronger anchoring can restrict adaptation, and that the best anchoring layer varies for individual source-target pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes trained on gold labels over frozen W2S reward-model representations: ANCHOR is 4.12/4.89/0.92 points above naive on HelpSteer3, Anthropic Helpful and UltraFeedback.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-label fine-tuning erodes preference-relevant linearly decodable information; representation anchoring preserves it.

fits_no_version.finding: CKA/CCA representation drift from the base model concentrates in middle and final layers. ANCHOR reduces drift, but the best checkpoint is not the least-drifted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation drift during W2S training relates to OOD transfer, in a controlled-drift sense.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Cross-dataset evaluation combines shifts in prompts, response styles and provenance, annotation protocols, and preference policies, so the study cannot isolate which factor causes OOD failures or establish representation drift as the sole cause. Evidence focuses on offline pairwise reward-model accuracy and a fixed set of helpful/harmless datasets and model scales; broader downstream evaluation is left for future work. Some reported transfer metrics are means over three seeds, but uncertainty for the main WRG/AOG/NTS table is not stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Not every per-method, per-source, per-target cell in Table 1 or full accuracy cell in Appendix Table 7 is separately recorded. Additional sweep and comparison cells from Tables 9–14 are also omitted where they repeat the same measured outcome; selected contrasting, negative, partial, and explicitly discussed results are retained above.

untested.parts: No sweep of supervisor or student size (one size pair per family); no chess or NLP-classification tasks; no predictor of PGR.
Strong students exploiting what the supervisor cannot check; whether gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike.

missing.what: Naive in-distribution PGR/WRG for the other 10 source×family cells (e.g. Qwen UltraFeedback -89.1%, Qwen RAIL -19.1%, Llama Anthropic Helpful 98.7%)
Confidence-based vs naive WRG/AOG across all 12 settings (roughly 6/12 better in-distribution)
Mean ID/OOD strong-ceiling gaps by method, and the decomposition into gold-transfer gap (5.22) and weak-supervision gap (naive 1.15, confidence 1.05, SEAM 2.83, ANCHOR 0.23)
Qwen/HelpSteer3 and Llama/RAIL weight-interpolation, early-stopping and LoRA-r8 controls; none restores positive Qwen source WRG
Best-of-4 reranking top-1 accuracy: ANCHOR 48.86 vs naive 45.17 (HelpSteer3 source)

record.verdict_notes: PGR is unstable here because Qwen strong ceilings are often within about 1 point of the weak teacher, or below it on some evaluation sets, producing values like 1.5k%. Prefer WRG for comparison. R34 and R35 take values from the Anthropic Helpful source block, not HelpSteer3. ANCHOR rows are the authors' own method; treat its V2 support with that in mind.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests weak-to-strong improvement in reward modeling, including PGR and comparisons with weak supervisors, for helpfulness and harmlessness datasets. It does not test other tasks or modalities.

Tests confidence-based W2S and several preservation/training variants, including A NCHOR, against naive W2S. It does not test ensembling weak supervisors or a broad sweep of weak-supervision loss variants.

Tests two model families, helpfulness and harmlessness preference categories, and representation-related probes. It does not test a broad range of scales, other task families such as chess, or whether representation measures predict PGR across a systematic sweep.

Tests cross-dataset preference-domain shift. It does not test strong students exploiting weaknesses a supervisor cannot check, or whether gains shrink specifically when weak and strong models make similar errors.
No theoretical conditions for students to outperform supervisors are derived or tested.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.
